text: Now the serpent was more cunning than any other creature of the field that the LORD God had made. The serpent said to the woman, "Did God really say you must not eat from any tree in the garden?"

versions.text: Now the serpent was more cunning than any other creature of the field that the LORD God had made. He said to the woman, "Did God really say you must not eat from any tree in the garden?"
versions.explanation: In the second sentence, the pronoun "He" follows immediately after "the LORD God," which can momentarily mislead a listener as to who is speaking. Naming the serpent removes the ambiguity for oral reading without lengthening the line awkwardly.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew opens with a disjunctive clause ("and the serpent, it was..."), which marks a shift of scene and introduces a new character; "Now the serpent..." renders this narrative pause. The adjective 'arum covers a range from admirable prudence to calculating slyness; "cunning" keeps the negative edge that the story goes on to justify, while other renderings choose "shrewd," "crafty," or "clever." Hebrew hayyat hassadeh means literally "living thing of the field," that is, a wild (non-domesticated) animal; "creature of the field" preserves the breadth of the phrase and reads more smoothly aloud than "beast." The Hebrew of the second sentence simply says "and he said to the woman," but for oral reading the subject is repeated as "The serpent said" so a listener does not lose track of who is speaking. The serpent's opening words, 'af ki, are notoriously hard to pin down: they can be read as a question ("Is it really the case that...?"), as a leading half-statement ("So God has said..."), or as feigned astonishment ("To think that God said..."). "Did God really say" captures the insinuating, probing tone that the woman's reply presupposes.

There is a deliberate sound-play between 'arum ("cunning") here and 'arummim ("naked") in the immediately preceding verse — the naked pair meet the shrewd one. The word for serpent, nahash, also resembles the verb nahash, "to practice divination," which may add an overtone of occult knowledge. The final phrase lo' tokhelu mikkol 'ets haggan is grammatically ambiguous: mikkol can mean "from any" (a sweeping prohibition) or "from all" (a partial one, "not from every tree"). The ambiguity is likely intentional, since the serpent's whole tactic is to exaggerate the divine command — God had in fact forbidden only one tree — and thereby make God appear stingy.

The narrative presents the serpent as one of the creatures God made, not as a rival deity; whatever evil it embodies, it is a creature and remains under God's ordering. Later Jewish and Christian tradition came to identify the serpent with Satan or the devil, but the text itself makes no such identification and leaves the source of its hostility unexplained. Note also that the serpent's method is neither force nor open denial but a question: it invites the woman to reconsider God's word, subtly reframing a single restriction as a comprehensive denial. Interpreters have long observed that the first temptation in Scripture is a temptation to distrust God's generosity.

In the wider ancient Near East the serpent was a charged symbol, associated variously with wisdom, healing, fertility, chaos, and immortality (as in the serpent that steals the plant of life in Mesopotamian epic), and it appeared on royal crowns and cult objects in Egypt and Canaan. An audience in that world would have heard "serpent" as more than a description of a snake in a garden; the story quietly demotes a revered symbol to the status of a mere field animal that God has made.

The ancient Greek tradition reads "of all the wild animals upon the earth" rather than "of the field," and some witnesses add "why?" or otherwise smooth the serpent's abrupt opening words — evidence that early translators also struggled with the difficult particles 'af ki. The Hebrew consonantal text is stable here, and the reading followed above requires no emendation.

text: The woman answered the serpent, "We may eat the fruit of the trees in the garden,

footnotes.text: Hebrew literally reads "From the fruit of the tree of the garden we will eat." The singular "tree" here is collective, covering the garden's trees as a whole, so it is rendered as a plural, "the trees in the garden." The verb form is a simple imperfect that can be read as a statement of fact ("we eat"), of intention ("we will eat"), or of permission; since the woman is reporting what God allows, "we may eat" best conveys the sense. The opening verb is simply "said," but because this is a reply to the serpent's question, "answered" is used for natural spoken rhythm. The verse ends with a comma and the quotation left open, because her sentence runs on without a break into the next verse.

The preposition on "fruit" (mi-) is partitive: "some of the fruit," not necessarily all of it. Her words deliberately echo the serpent's phrase "any tree of the garden" from the previous verse, but she drops his sweeping negative "not from any" and reverses it into a positive permission. Hebrew has no separate form here to mark "may"; the plain imperfect carries whatever modal shading the context supplies.

The woman corrects the serpent's distortion, yet her own wording is noticeably thinner than the original command, which used an emphatic doubled verb, "you may surely eat," and stressed "every tree." By stating the permission flatly and (in the next verse) adding a prohibition on touching, the reply quietly shrinks God's generosity and enlarges his restriction. Interpreters differ on whether this reflects careless memory, the serpent's influence, or a hint that the command had been passed on to her secondhand.

text: but about the fruit of the tree in the middle of the garden God said, 'You must not eat from it or touch it, or you will die.'"

footnotes.text: The Hebrew opens with a phrase set off by the connector "and from the fruit of the tree," which is here rendered "but about the fruit" to mark the contrast with the permission granted in the previous verse; the sentence in Hebrew places the object first for emphasis. The clause "pen-temutun" is literally "lest you die" — a warning of possible consequence rather than a flat prediction. Since "lest" is stiff in spoken English, this reading uses "or you will die," which keeps the rhythm of a single spoken sentence and sets up the serpent's blunt denial in the next verse. Quotation marks are supplied (Hebrew has none): the outer marks continue the woman's speech begun in verse 2, and the inner marks enclose her report of God's command.

The verb form "temutun" carries an extra final -n (called paragogic nun), an older or more formal ending on the plural imperfect; it lends the line a solemn, weighty sound and reappears in the serpent's reply in verse 4, so that the two lines echo each other. The particle "pen" always introduces something feared or to be avoided. Note also that in the original prohibition the wording was emphatic — an infinitive absolute doubling the verb, "dying you shall die" — whereas here the woman uses the simple verb, without that intensifying doubling. The phrase "in the middle of the garden" (be-tokh ha-gan) does not name the tree, as if avoiding the words "knowledge of good and evil."

The woman's quotation differs from the command as first given: it adds "or touch it," leaves out the freedom-affirming "you may freely eat of every tree," omits the tree's name, and softens the emphatic certainty of death. Interpreters have read this in opposite ways — either as a well-meant strengthening of the fence around the command, or as the first slippage in which generous permission is remembered as harsh restriction. Either way, the conversation is already reshaping the word it repeats. Notice also that both serpent and woman speak of "God" (Elohim) rather than the covenant name used by the narrator, which some see as a subtle distancing.

Ancient Near Eastern legal and religious speech often extended a prohibition to include contact as well as consumption, since touching a forbidden or holy thing could itself transmit guilt or defilement — a pattern later visible in Israel's laws about holy mountains and sacred objects. Hearers in that world would recognize "do not touch" as the natural way to guard something dangerous or set apart, whether or not it was part of the original wording.

Some ancient witnesses smooth the sentence by repeating "you shall not eat of the fruit of the tree," and a few harmonize the woman's words more closely with the command as originally given, including the emphatic "you shall surely die." The shorter, slightly uneven wording preserved in the traditional Hebrew text is followed here, since the differences between command and quotation are likely intentional.

text: The serpent said to the woman, "You will certainly not die."

versions.text: "You will not die," the serpent said to the woman.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew uses the emphatic infinitive absolute (לֹא־מוֹת תְּמֻתוּן), a deliberate echo and contradiction of the earlier warning; rendering it simply as "You will not die" loses that emphasis. Placing the speech attribution first also reads more naturally aloud and leads smoothly into the continued speech in the next verse.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew has an emphatic construction: the infinitive absolute מוֹת placed before the finite verb תְּמֻתוּן, literally "dying you shall die." The negative לֹא stands in front of the whole phrase. Two renderings are possible: "You will certainly not die" (the negation covers the emphasis) or "You will not surely die" (the serpent denies only the certainty, leaving room for doubt). The rendering chosen here takes the serpent's words as a flat, confident contradiction, which fits the tone of what follows in verse 5, where he explains what will really happen. The alternative, more insinuating reading is defensible and preferred by some, but it is harder to say aloud without sounding ambiguous.

The serpent's words are a deliberate echo of the divine warning in 2:17, מוֹת תָּמוּת, "you shall surely die" — the same infinitive-absolute construction, now simply prefixed with לֹא. He also picks up the plural form the woman used in the previous verse (תְּמֻתוּן, with the archaic or emphatic final nun, sometimes called paragogic nun, common in solemn or poetic speech). Word order is significant: in Hebrew the negative particle normally stands immediately before the finite verb, so placing לֹא before the infinitive absolute is unusual and has fed the long debate over exactly how much of the statement is being denied.

This is the first direct contradiction of God's word in Scripture, and later tradition reads it as the archetypal lie (compare the description of the devil as a liar from the beginning in John 8:44). Interpreters have long noted that the serpent's claim proves partly true on the surface — the couple do not drop dead that day — which raises the question of what kind of death God meant: immediate physical death, mortality entering the human condition, or estrangement from God as the source of life. Most readings hold that the sentence of death is real but unfolds over time, so that the serpent's statement is a half-truth, more dangerous than an outright falsehood.

Speaking serpents and serpent figures associated with wisdom, secret knowledge, immortality, and the loss of it are widespread in the ancient Near East; in the Gilgamesh epic a snake steals the plant of life. Here, however, the serpent is explicitly one of the creatures God made (3:1), not a rival deity, and the narrative gives no cosmic status to him. The wordplay between נָחָשׁ ("serpent") and עָרוּם ("shrewd") in verse 1 marks him as clever rather than divine.

The consonantal text is stable across the Hebrew witnesses. The early Greek translation renders the emphatic construction woodenly as "not by death shall you die," preserving the infinitive absolute with a dative noun; the Aramaic versions likewise keep the doubled verb. None of the ancient versions resolves the ambiguity about the scope of the negation.

text: "For God knows that on the day you eat from it your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil."

footnotes.text: The Hebrew opens with כִּי ("for, because"), continuing the serpent's speech from the previous verse, so the rendering keeps it as a single flowing argument rather than starting a new thought. "On the day you eat" translates the idiom בְּיוֹם אֲכָלְכֶם literally; the phrase commonly means simply "when" or "as soon as," and some renderings say "when you eat." The literal wording is retained here because it echoes the identical phrase in the warning of 2:17 and lets the reader hear the serpent twisting God's own words. The Hebrew joins the clauses with a simple "and" ("and your eyes will be opened, and you will be..."); the first "and" is left untranslated for smoother English rhythm. כֵּאלֹהִים could be rendered "like God," "like a god," "like gods," or "like divine beings"; "like God" is chosen for consistency with the narrative's use of אֱלֹהִים for the Creator throughout these chapters, though the ambiguity is genuine.

The verb נִפְקְחוּ is a passive (niphal) form of פָּקַח, a verb used almost exclusively of opening eyes or ears — especially the eyes of the blind. It suggests sudden new perception rather than mere waking. The participle יֹדְעֵי ("knowing, those who know") is masculine plural and agrees grammatically with the plural form אֱלֹהִים, which is one reason the phrase can be read either as "like God, who knows" or "like gods, who know." The pairing "good and evil" (טוֹב וָרָע) is a merism, two opposites standing for the whole range between them, and so can denote comprehensive knowledge or the capacity to decide for oneself what is beneficial and what is harmful.

The serpent's claim is not simply a lie: in 3:7 their eyes are indeed opened, and in 3:22 God says, "the man has become like one of us, knowing good and evil." What is false is the framing — that God withholds this knowledge out of jealousy, and that grasping it will bring life rather than death. Interpreters have long debated what the knowledge of good and evil is: moral discernment, mature wisdom, sexual awareness, or autonomous authority to define right and wrong apart from God. Many read the temptation as the desire to be like God in the wrong way — seizing by grasp what could only be received as gift — and this verse has accordingly been central to Christian reflection on the nature of sin as pride and self-assertion.

In the wider ancient Near East, wisdom and the knowledge of good and evil were regularly portrayed as marks of divinity, and stories of humans reaching for immortality or divine knowledge and losing it were widespread. Serpents in that world were ambiguous figures, associated with wisdom, healing, fertility, and chaos alike. The narrative uses these familiar associations but sharply reworks them: the serpent is not a god or a rival deity but a creature of the field, and the boundary it invites the humans to cross is a moral one set by their Creator.

text: The woman saw that the tree was good for food, that it was a delight to the eyes, and that it was desirable for gaining wisdom. So she took some of its fruit and ate, and she gave some to her husband, who was with her, and he ate.

versions.text: The woman saw that the tree was good for food, that it was a delight to the eyes, and that it was desirable for the wisdom it would give. So she took some of its fruit and ate, and she gave some to her husband, who was with her, and he ate.
versions.explanation: "desirable for the wisdom it would give" is a bit wordy and breaks the rhythm of the three parallel clauses; "desirable for gaining wisdom" keeps the same sense of the Hebrew infinitive ("to make wise") while matching the shorter cadence of "good for food" and "a delight to the eyes," which reads better aloud.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew phrase נֶחְמָד הָעֵץ לְהַשְׂכִּיל literally reads "the tree was desirable to make wise" or "to give insight." The rendering "desirable for gaining wisdom" keeps the sense of the causative verb while reading smoothly aloud. Some render it "desirable to make one wise," others "to be looked at" — an ancient reading that took the verb from a different root meaning "to gaze." The wisdom sense is preferred here, since it links directly with the serpent's promise in verse 5. The verse builds in three parallel clauses, each introduced by "that," and the translation preserves that triple rhythm rather than collapsing them. "Some of its fruit" reflects the partitive Hebrew preposition (literally "from its fruit"), and the same partitive sense carries into "gave some to her husband." The phrase "who was with her" translates a single Hebrew word, עִמָּהּ, placed here as a relative clause so the line does not stumble in reading.

The three descriptions form an ascending sequence: good for food (appetite), a delight to the eyes (beauty), desirable for wisdom (ambition). The word תַּאֲוָה ("delight, desire, craving") is elsewhere used of appetite and longing, sometimes with a negative shading of covetousness. The verb לְהַשְׂכִּיל comes from the root שׂכל, associated with prudence, insight and success — the same root that names the wise person in the wisdom writings. There is also a subtle wordplay across the chapter: the serpent is described as עָרוּם ("shrewd") in verse 1, and in verse 7 the pair discover they are עֵירֻמִּים ("naked") — the sound is nearly identical. The chain of quick past-tense verbs — saw, took, ate, gave — moves with deliberate speed, and the Hebrew narrative form gives the whole act a single breathless motion.

This verse is the pivot of the chapter and, in much Christian reading, the moment of the first human transgression. The threefold description of the tree has long been read as a pattern of temptation: bodily craving, visual allure, and the desire for what elevates one's status. Interpreters differ over the man's role: the words "who was with her" have been taken by some to mean he stood beside her throughout the exchange with the serpent and remained silent, which sharpens his responsibility; others read it more loosely as simply indicating he was present when she offered the fruit. Note also that the text says nothing of the fruit's species, nothing of the woman being deceived beyond what the narrative shows, and offers no explicit judgment here — the narrator reports the act plainly and lets the consequences speak.

Ancient Near Eastern literature contains other accounts of humanity losing immortality or gaining knowledge through eating, and readers have long compared this scene to such stories, though the differences are as striking as the similarities. The identification of the fruit with an apple is a later Western tradition, likely encouraged by a Latin pun between the words for "evil" and "apple"; Jewish tradition variously suggested the fig, the grape, or wheat. The fig appears in the very next verse, which may have prompted that association.

text: Then the eyes of both of them were opened, and they knew that they were naked. So they sewed fig leaves together and made loincloths for themselves.

versions.text: Then the eyes of both of them were opened, and they knew they were naked. So they sewed fig leaves together and made coverings for themselves.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew "chagorot" denotes something girded about the waist \u2014 loincloths or girdles \u2014 rather than the vaguer "coverings." Adding "that" after "knew" also gives the clause a smoother cadence for oral reading.

footnotes.text: "Loincloths" renders Hebrew ḥagorot, from the root meaning "to gird." The word denotes something bound around the waist rather than full clothing; older renderings such as "aprons" or "girdles" capture the same idea, while "coverings" is looser. The choice of "loincloths" keeps the item modest in scope, which matters because God later provides fuller garments of skin. "Sewed... together" reflects the Hebrew verb for stitching; the singular collective 'aleh te'enah (literally "fig leaf") is rendered as a plural "fig leaves" in keeping with English usage. "Then" at the head of the verse marks the sequence of the narrative waw-consecutive, tying the opening of their eyes directly to the eating in the previous verse.

The verb paqaḥ, "to open," is used almost exclusively of opening eyes (or ears), often of restoring sight to the blind. Its passive form here leaves the agent unnamed, an understatement that lets the reader supply the cause. The verse turns on wordplay: 'arummim, "naked," echoes 'arum, "crafty," used of the serpent earlier in the chapter, and it recalls the couple's earlier state of being naked and unashamed. The serpent's promise that "your eyes will be opened" is fulfilled in words but not in substance — what they come to know is themselves.

The opening of the eyes is the serpent's promise fulfilled ironically: knowledge arrives, but as self-consciousness and shame rather than divine wisdom. Interpreters differ on what is gained — moral discernment, sexual awareness, adult autonomy, or simply the bitter experience of guilt. The homemade covering is widely read as the first act of self-remedy for sin: real but inadequate, and soon replaced by a covering God himself provides. Many readers see here the birth of shame as the human condition, and of hiding as its natural expression, continued in the next verse.

The fig is among the earliest cultivated fruits of the ancient Near East, and its leaves are unusually broad and sturdy — a plausible improvised material, though rough against the skin. Some traditions identified the fig as the forbidden tree itself, since it is the only tree named in the chapter apart from the tree of life and the tree of knowledge. In the ancient world nakedness was associated with poverty, captivity, and humiliation; to be stripped bare was to be exposed and defenseless, which sharpens the couple's urge to cover themselves.

text: They heard the sound of the LORD God walking in the garden in the cool of the day, and the man and his wife hid from the presence of the LORD God among the trees of the garden.

footnotes.text: Hebrew qôl means both "sound" and "voice." Since the participle that follows ("walking about") describes movement rather than speech, "the sound of the LORD God walking" is the most natural reading, and it prepares for God's first spoken words in the next verse. Older renderings have "the voice of the LORD God," and grammatically the participle could also be taken with "the LORD God" rather than with "sound" ("they heard the LORD God, walking in the garden"); a few interpreters even read qôl of thunder. The phrase rendered "in the cool of the day" is literally "at the breeze of the day," the evening wind that relieves the heat; ancient renderings supported "toward evening" or "in the afternoon." "Among the trees" translates a Hebrew singular used collectively, literally "in the midst of the tree of the garden." "From the presence of" renders an idiom that is literally "from the face of."

The verb mithallēk is a reflexive-iterative form of hālak, "to go": to walk to and fro, stroll about at ease. The same form describes God's presence moving among his people in the wilderness camp and tabernacle traditions, so the picture is one of familiar, habitual companionship now broken. Note also the sound-play of fear: the man who was ʿārôm ("naked") now hides (yitḥabbēʾ) among the ʿēṣ ("tree/trees") of the garden, the very trees whose fruit brought him to this point. Rûaḥ hayyôm literally joins "wind/breath/spirit" with "day"; the same noun rûaḥ appears in Genesis for the wind or Spirit of God, and here it marks a time of day by its breeze.

The verse is boldly anthropomorphic: God walks, is heard, and can apparently be hidden from. Interpreters have read this in various ways — as a genuine narrative of divine nearness in the garden, as accommodating human language for God's manifest presence, or (in some ancient Jewish and Christian readings) as a theophany of the Word. The theological force is the reversal it records: the presence that should have been welcomed is now dreaded, and the first effect of sin is not punishment but flight. Yet the hiding is futile, and God's approach in the following verse shows that he comes seeking before he comes judging — a pattern later readers saw fulfilled in God's continued search for the lost.

In the ancient Near East the late-afternoon and evening breeze was the pleasant part of the day, when work eased and people walked or received guests; royal gardens were designed for just such strolling. Depicting a deity walking in a garden park would evoke for early hearers the image of a king in his estate, with the man and woman as gardeners who owe him an accounting. Hiding among dense garden foliage was a realistic reflex, and clothing oneself and hiding from a superior's face both belonged to the vocabulary of shame and vassal fear.

The consonantal text is stable. The early Greek tradition specifies the time as "toward evening/afternoon," and the Latin as "at the breeze after midday," both interpreting the Hebrew "breeze of the day." The Aramaic paraphrases characteristically soften the anthropomorphism, speaking of the "voice of the word of the LORD" walking in the garden. Some manuscripts and versions read the plural "trees of the garden" where the Hebrew has the collective singular.

text: Then the LORD God called to the man and said to him, "Where are you?"

versions.text: But the LORD God called to the man and said to him, "Where are you?"
versions.explanation: The Hebrew waw-consecutive here is simple narrative sequence; rendering it "But" imports an adversative contrast not present in the text. "Then" preserves the narrative flow from the hiding in verse 8 and reads naturally aloud.

footnotes.text: The opening "Then" renders the Hebrew narrative verb chain (wayyiqtol), which simply links this action to the preceding scene; older renderings often used "And." "Called to the man" reflects the verb qara' with the preposition 'el, which regularly means to call out toward someone, i.e. to summon or hail, rather than merely "call" or "name." Hebrew ha'adam carries the article throughout this chapter and is therefore rendered "the man" rather than as the personal name Adam; the wordplay with 'adamah ("ground," v. 19) depends on this generic sense. The question is kept as a bare "Where are you?" without any interpretive expansion such as "Why are you hiding?", since the Hebrew is a single compact word.

The whole question is one word in Hebrew: 'ayyekkah, formed from the interrogative 'ayyeh ("where?") plus the second-person masculine singular suffix, lengthened here into a pausal form because it stands at the end of the verse. The address is singular, spoken to the man alone, even though both had hidden (v. 8). Written without vowels, the consonants of 'ayyekkah are identical to 'ekah, "How...!", the opening cry of Hebrew funeral laments; ancient interpreters heard in this a deliberate echo, as though God's first question to fallen humanity were already a dirge.

God's question is not a request for information; the narrative has already told us where the couple are. It functions as a summons that draws the hidden into the open, initiating dialogue rather than immediate sentence. Interpreters have read it variously as an act of judgment (the accused is called to account), as an act of grace (God seeks the sinner before the sinner seeks God), and as a diagnostic question about the human condition: the man has lost not his location but his place before God. Note the sequence: God speaks first, and the interrogation that follows (vv. 9-13) precedes the curses (vv. 14-19).

Some early witnesses expand the address by supplying the name, reading in effect "Adam, where are you?", a reading reflected in parts of the Greek and Syriac traditions and widely echoed in later quotation. The Hebrew text has only the pronoun-suffixed question, and the article on ha'adam earlier in the verse supports the shorter reading.

text: He answered, "I heard your voice in the garden, and I was afraid, because I was naked; so I hid."

versions.text: He answered, "I heard you in the garden, and I was afraid, because I was naked; so I hid."
versions.explanation: The Hebrew reads אֶת־קֹלְךָ שָׁמַעְתִּי, "I heard your voice (or sound)," not merely "I heard you." Restoring "your voice" preserves the concrete imagery of the man reacting to the sound of God moving in the garden, and it reads well aloud.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew places the object first — literally "Your voice I heard in the garden" — a word order that throws the weight onto "your voice." English cannot easily front the object without sounding stilted, so the emphasis is carried instead by the unbroken forward motion of the sentence. The noun qol can mean either "voice" or "sound"; "sound" would tie this line to the "sound of the LORD God walking in the garden" in verse 8, but "voice" is retained here because God has just spoken (verse 9), and because the man is answering a spoken question. The three verbs "I heard... I was afraid... I hid" are joined in Hebrew by simple sequential connectives; the rendering "and... because... so" makes the chain of cause and consequence audible for a listener, where Hebrew leaves it implied.

The word for "naked" here is 'erom, a different form from the 'arummim of 2:25, where the couple were naked "and not ashamed." The shift in vocabulary marks a shift in condition. Both stand close in sound to 'arum, "crafty," used of the serpent in 3:1 — a play in which cunning and nakedness echo one another. The pronoun 'anokhi ("I") is the longer, weightier form of the first person, which lends a self-conscious insistence to "I was naked." Note also that where verse 8 uses a reflexive stem for hiding ("hid himself"), this verse uses a simple passive-reflexive form, "I hid" or "I was hidden."

This is the first mention of fear in Scripture, and the first human speech addressed to God. The man answers truthfully but not fully: he names the fear and the nakedness, but says nothing of the tree or the eating — which is precisely why God's next question must press further (verse 11). Nakedness, once a state of unashamed openness, has become the reason for flight. Interpreters have long asked whether the man's fear is guilt over disobedience, dread of judgment, or simply the shame of exposure; the text lets all three stand together, and later biblical language of being clothed or covered before God draws on this scene.

In the ancient Near East, public nakedness was associated with shame, poverty, captivity, and loss of standing; captives and the destitute were commonly depicted stripped. Clothing signified belonging, status, and dignity. The man's excuse would therefore have sounded plausible to ancient hearers: to be seen unclothed by one's Lord was a genuine disgrace, not merely a private embarrassment.

The Greek tradition expands the line to read "I heard your voice as you walked in the garden," harmonizing it with the description in verse 8. The Hebrew text as preserved has no such addition, and the shorter reading is followed here.

text: And God said, "Who told you that you are naked? Have you eaten from the tree I commanded you not to eat from?"

footnotes.text: The Hebrew opens simply "And he said," with no named subject; the speaker is the LORD God, who has been questioning the man since verse 9. Because the surrounding verses alternate speakers rapidly, the name "God" is supplied here so that a listener hearing the passage read aloud can immediately tell who is speaking. The second question is more emphatic in Hebrew than in English: it fronts the prepositional phrase, literally "Was it from the tree that I commanded you not to eat from it — you ate?" That word order could be rendered "Was it from the tree… that you ate?" but the plain yes-or-no question reads more naturally aloud while keeping the same force. Hebrew also repeats the pronoun after the relative clause ("the tree… from it"), a normal feature of Hebrew relative constructions that English drops; ending the clause with "from" preserves the spoken rhythm.

"Told" renders the verb higgid (causative of nagad), "to declare, make known, report" — the same verb used for announcing news. The question is literally "Who made it known to you…?", implying that awareness of nakedness is information the man should not have had. "Naked" here is 'erom, a form that echoes 'arum, "crafty," used of the serpent in 3:1, and stands in tension with 'arummim in 2:25, where the couple were naked and unashamed. The prohibition is expressed by the infinitive with lebilti, a strong negative construction: "so as not to eat." All the pronouns and verb forms addressed to the man are masculine singular.

The two questions are rhetorical: God is not gathering information but drawing out confession. The first exposes the symptom (shame at nakedness) and the second names the cause (eating from the forbidden tree). By phrasing the charge as a question rather than an accusation, the narrative gives the man an opening to admit what he has done — an opening he uses instead to shift blame in the next verse. Interpreters have long noted that God's questioning here follows a pattern of merciful interrogation seen elsewhere in Scripture, where the guilty are invited to speak before judgment is announced.

The exchange mirrors the pattern of a legal inquiry in the ancient Near East, where a judge or overlord confronts a subject with questions establishing both the fact and the awareness of wrongdoing before pronouncing sentence. Nakedness in that cultural setting carried strong connotations of shame, defenselessness and loss of status; a person stripped bare was one exposed to judgment or reduced to captivity, which sharpens the force of the man's self-awareness.

The Hebrew text of this verse is stable in the manuscript tradition. Some ancient versions smooth the double question into a single sentence, joining the clauses with "unless" — "Who told you that you are naked, unless you ate from the tree…" — which reflects an interpretive rendering of the interrogative particle rather than a different underlying text.

versions.text: And God said, "Who told you that you were naked? Have you eaten from the tree I commanded you not to eat from?"
versions.explanation: The Hebrew clause כִּי עֵירֹם אָתָּה is a nominal clause in the present: "that you are naked." The past-tense "were" shifts the focus to a former condition, whereas the point is the man's present state of exposure, which he has just confessed in verse 10. The verse's own linguistic footnote renders it "Who told you that you are naked...?", so the present tense also brings the text into line with its annotation and reads just as smoothly aloud.

text: The man said, "The woman you gave to be with me—she gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate."

versions.text: The man said, "The woman you put here with me—she gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate."
versions.explanation: The Hebrew repeats the same verb (נָתַתָּה … נָתְנָה): 'the woman you gave … she gave me.' Rendering the first verb as 'put here' loses this deliberate echo, which is central to the man's shifting of blame. 'You gave to be with me' also matches עִמָּדִי more closely than the added 'here,' and the repeated 'gave … gave' reads well aloud.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew says simply "she gave me from the tree, and I ate"; the word "fruit" is supplied for clarity, since English cannot easily speak of eating "from a tree." The phrase "you gave to be with me" renders a Hebrew expression that literally reads "whom you gave with me" (or "beside me"), echoing the divine intention of 2:18 that the woman be a companion alongside the man. The dash reproduces a Hebrew construction in which the subject is announced first and then picked up again by an emphatic pronoun — "the woman... she" — which in oral reading gives the pause and the pointing finger that the sentence requires. The closing "and I ate" is deliberately kept short and identical to the woman's words in the next verse, since the Hebrew uses exactly the same two words in both places.

The preposition in "with me" is the fuller, somewhat weightier form of the ordinary Hebrew word for "with," carrying the sense of "at my side, in my company." The pronoun "she" is grammatically unnecessary — the verb already marks the subject — so its presence throws the stress onto the woman: "she is the one who gave." Note also the tight sound-play of the repeated root for "give": "whom you gave... she gave to me." The verb form translated "and I ate" is the standard narrative past, and its brevity after the long, winding excuse is part of the effect.

The man's answer is famously evasive: it moves from the woman to the God who provided her, so that the blame travels upward before it ever reaches himself. Interpreters have long noted that the gift of 2:18–23, received with joy and poetry, is here recast as the cause of ruin. Yet the sentence does end in confession — "and I ate" — and readers differ over whether this is genuine admission or merely the minimum extracted under questioning. The parallel with the woman's reply in v. 13 sets up a chain of deflected responsibility that the judgments of vv. 14–19 will nonetheless assign to each party in turn.

The exchange is shaped like a judicial inquiry: the questions of vv. 9, 11 and 13 function as an interrogation, and the accused answer in turn before sentence is passed. Ancient Near Eastern legal practice knew such a sequence of summons, charge, response and verdict, and the narrative uses its rhythms to frame the scene in the garden as a trial rather than a mere conversation.

In the Pentateuch the feminine pronoun "she" is regularly written with the consonants of the masculine form and read as feminine; the traditional pointing here marks that reading. The Samaritan tradition writes the expected feminine spelling. The ancient versions agree with the Hebrew throughout the verse, with some witnesses making explicit the object "the fruit" that the Hebrew leaves implied.

text: Then the LORD God said to the woman, "What is this you have done?" The woman answered, "The serpent deceived me, and I ate."

footnotes.text: The question "What is this you have done?" renders Hebrew mah-zōʾt ʿāśît literally; it is an exclamation of accusation rather than a request for information, and could also be rendered "What have you done?" or, more idiomatically, "Why have you done this?" The verb hiššîʾanî is translated "deceived me"; alternatives include "tricked," "misled," "beguiled," or "lured me on." "The woman answered" renders the same verb (wattōʾmer, "said") used for God's speech, but English rhythm and the question-and-answer structure make "answered" the natural choice for oral reading. Note that the woman, unlike the man in verse 12, does not name God as the source of the tempter, though she too deflects responsibility; the translation keeps her reply as terse in English as it is in Hebrew — five words for four.

The verb hiššîʾanî is the hiphil of nāšāʾ (a homonym of the common verb "to lift"), meaning to lead astray or delude. Its sound plays against han-nāḥāš, "the serpent": han-nāḥāš hiššîʾanî, a clipped hiss of repeated sibilants that mimics the creature named. The Hebrew of both replies ends with the identical word wāʾōkēl, "and I ate" — the man's confession in verse 12 and the woman's here close on the same syllable, so that the one undeniable fact is repeated while the blame is passed along.

The chain of evasion — man blames woman, woman blames serpent — is a central feature of the narrative: guilt is acknowledged in act ("and I ate") but never in responsibility. Later interpreters read the woman's claim of deception in different ways: some as an honest account, since deception was indeed practiced upon her, others as an excuse that does not excuse, since the command had been clearly known. Early Christian writers took up the language of deception in describing her experience, and the theme became bound up with debates over the transmission of sin and the relative culpability of the two.

Talking, cunning serpents appear widely in ancient Near Eastern lore, often associated with wisdom, chaos, healing, or immortality — the shedding of skin suggesting renewal of life. In this account the serpent is not a rival deity but one of the creatures God made, which is why the questioning stops with the woman: God interrogates the human pair, who were addressed by command, but simply sentences the serpent in the following verse without inviting a reply.

The consonantal Hebrew text is stable here; ancient Greek and Syriac witnesses agree in substance, rendering the verb with words for "deceived" or "led astray." Some witnesses smooth the divine speech with a connective such as "and," and a few Greek copies expand the woman's reply by adding "the serpent, which you made" or similar, apparently by assimilation to the man's answer in verse 12; the shorter reading is preferred.

text: Then the LORD God said to the serpent, "Because you have done this, cursed are you above all livestock and above every beast of the field. On your belly you shall crawl, and dust you shall eat all the days of your life.

versions.text: So the LORD God said to the serpent, "Because you have done this, you are cursed above all livestock and above every creature of the field. On your belly you shall crawl, and dust you shall eat all the days of your life.
versions.explanation: Two small improvements for rhythm and fidelity: (1) The Hebrew fronts the curse word (\u05d0\u05e8\u05d5\u05e8 \u05d0\u05ea\u05d4), and "cursed are you" preserves that emphatic word order while reading more strongly aloud than the flatter "you are cursed"; (2) \u05d7\u05d9\u05ea \u05d4\u05e9\u05d3\u05d4 is the standard "beast of the field," which is more concrete than "creature" and pairs better with "livestock." Also, "Then" keeps the narrative connective consistent with the preceding verse's rendering of the same \u05d5\u05d9\u05d0\u05de\u05e8 formula.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew verb telekh simply means "you shall go/walk"; the translation renders it "crawl" because the phrase "on your belly you shall go" describes locomotion without legs, and "crawl" preserves that sense for the ear. The preposition min in "cursed are you above all livestock" can be comparative ("more than all") or separative ("apart from, away from"), which would yield "cursed and banished from all the livestock and from every beast of the field." The comparative reading is chosen here as the more natural sense of a curse formula and the one that matches the parallel "and above every beast of the field." The opening "Because you have done this" renders ki asita zot; note that God asks the serpent no question, unlike the man and the woman, so the sentence follows immediately.

The word for "belly," gachon, is rare, appearing elsewhere in the Hebrew Bible only in the food laws concerning creatures that move on their belly, which strengthens the link between this sentence and the categories of clean and unclean animals. "Dust you shall eat" is an idiom of utter humiliation and defeat: enemies are elsewhere said to lick the dust, and a later prophet pictures nations trembling and licking dust like serpents. Note also the chain of catchwords running through the chapter: the serpent was arum (crafty) and is now arur (cursed), a sound-play that turns his cleverness into his sentence.

The curse falls first on the serpent and, unlike the words to the woman and the man, involves no dialogue and no possibility of reply. Interpreters differ on the scope: some read this as an account of why snakes go legless and are loathed, others as a symbolic description of a spiritual adversary brought low, and many as both at once, since the narrative treats the serpent as a real creature that speaks. Crucially, the ground and the human pair are addressed with hardship, but only the serpent is directly cursed, which shapes the whole biblical pattern of judgment aimed at the tempter rather than the tempted.

In the surrounding cultures of the ancient Near East the serpent carried heavy symbolic freight: a sign of wisdom, healing, fertility, immortality and royal protection in Egypt, and of chaos in Mesopotamian myth. Against that background this verse is strikingly deflationary: the serpent is not a god or a rival power but a creature among the livestock and wild animals, subject to the Creator's sentence. The flickering tongue of a snake touching the ground would readily suggest to ancient observers the image of an animal feeding on dust.

An early Greek tradition reads "on your breast and belly you shall go," expanding the single Hebrew word for belly, and has "every beast of the earth" rather than "of the field." These are best explained as clarifying or harmonizing renderings; the received Hebrew text is well supported and is followed here.

text: And I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your offspring and hers; he will strike your head, and you will strike his heel."

versions.text: And I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your offspring and hers; he will crush your head, and you will strike his heel."
versions.explanation: The Hebrew repeats the same verb ("shuf") in both clauses, and the parallelism is part of the verse's force and rhythm. Rendering it first as "crush" and then as "strike" obscures the deliberate repetition; using one verb for both preserves the balanced cadence for oral reading while remaining faithful to the wordplay.

footnotes.text: The verb שׁוּף (shuf) occurs twice, and the translation renders it identically both times — "strike" — because Hebrew deliberately uses the same word for what the offspring does to the serpent's head and what the serpent does to the heel. Other renderings include "bruise," "crush," and "lie in wait for"; "crush" fits a blow to the head but strains the parallel blow to the heel, so a neutral verb preserves the symmetry the Hebrew builds. "Offspring" translates זֶרַע (zera', literally "seed"), a collective singular that can mean a single descendant or a whole line of descendants; "seed" is more literal but reads oddly in oral English. The pronoun הוּא is grammatically masculine singular, agreeing with the collective noun, and is rendered "he" (rather than "it" or "they") to keep that singular force; "hers" is used for "her offspring" to avoid repeating the noun in a line meant to be heard aloud.

אֵיבָה ('eyvah, "enmity, hostility") is from the same root as אוֹיֵב, "enemy" — it denotes settled, personal hostility rather than a passing quarrel. The verb אָשִׁית ("I will put/set") places God himself as the one establishing this conflict. "Head" (רֹאשׁ) and "heel" (עָקֵב) stand without prepositions, functioning as accusatives of place: "strike you as to the head... strike him as to the heel." The two body parts are chosen for contrast: the vulnerable, fatal point and the low, reachable point. There is also assonance in יְשׁוּפְךָ / תְּשׁוּפֶנּוּ, a mirrored pair of verbs that makes the mutual wounding audible.

This verse has been read since antiquity as the first announcement of good news — the so-called protoevangelium — with the singular "he" pointing to one descendant of the woman who defeats the serpent. Others read זֶרַע collectively: humanity as a whole, or the covenant line, in ongoing struggle with evil. The asymmetry of the two blows (head versus heel) has been taken to imply decisive defeat for the serpent and only wounding for the offspring, though the identical verb keeps the outcome understated in the Hebrew itself. Both readings can be held together: a corporate conflict that culminates in an individual.

Early Greek translation rendered the pronoun with a masculine form even though the Greek word for "seed" is neuter, suggesting an individual rather than a collective was already in view among ancient readers. Some later Latin transmission read a feminine pronoun ("she will strike"), which shaped centuries of Western art and devotion, but the Hebrew consonants and vowels support a masculine subject.

In the ancient Near East the serpent carried associations with fertility, chaos, wisdom, and immortality, and appeared as a guardian figure in temple and royal iconography. A word placing a hereditary curse and endless enmity on such a creature would have been heard as a demotion of a revered symbol. Snakebite on the foot was a real hazard for barefoot or sandaled agricultural workers, which gives the image of the struck heel its everyday force.

text: To the woman he said, "I will greatly increase your pain in childbearing; in pain you will give birth to children. Your desire will be for your husband, and he will rule over you."

footnotes.text: The Hebrew doubles the verb ("multiplying I will multiply"), an emphatic construction rendered here as "I will greatly increase." The following words are literally "your pain and your conception"; the two nouns are best taken together as a single idea (a hendiadys), hence "your pain in childbearing." Alternative renderings keep them separate: "your toil and your pregnancies" or "your pangs and your conceiving." The verse ends with "Your desire will be for your husband" — a smooth-flowing rendering of a terse Hebrew clause with no verb, literally "and toward your husband your desire." Some read the preposition as adversarial ("your desire will be against your husband"), and others take the noun as "turning" rather than "desire." The final clause is straightforward: "he will rule over you."

The noun rendered "pain" (itstsabon) occurs only three times in the Bible, twice in this chapter — here of the woman and again in verse 17 of the man's labor in the field. The shared vocabulary links the two sentences: the same hardship touches the woman's work of bringing forth life and the man's work of drawing food from the soil. The word rendered "desire" (teshuqah) is even rarer, appearing only here, in the next chapter concerning sin "crouching at the door," and once in a love poem. Its rarity is why translators differ so widely. The verb "rule" (mashal) is the ordinary word for governing or having dominion, not a word for tyranny in itself.

Notice that the woman herself is not cursed; the curse falls on the serpent and on the ground. What she receives is a description of altered conditions. Interpreters divide over whether "he will rule over you" states a divine command establishing an enduring order, or describes a distortion of the original mutuality of the man and woman — a consequence of the fall rather than a design for it. Those who read it descriptively point out that the same sentence announces pain and death, which no one takes as commanded ideals. Those who read it as normative appeal to the shape of the household in later biblical instruction. The rare word "desire" also carries interpretive weight: it can mean longing and attachment, or a striving after control that the man answers with domination.

In the ancient world childbirth was among the most dangerous events in a woman's life; skeletal remains and burial evidence from the region show high maternal and infant mortality. A woman's labor also included the exhausting round of grinding, weaving, hauling water, and bearing and nursing children — labor essential to a household's survival. The sentence spoken here would have described daily reality for its first hearers, not an abstraction.

The ancient Greek translation reads "your pains and your groaning," apparently understanding the second noun differently from the traditional Hebrew vowels, and it renders "desire" as "turning" — a reading echoed in some early Syriac and Latin witnesses. The consonantal Hebrew text is stable across the manuscript tradition; the variations reflect different vocalizations and interpretations rather than differing texts.

text: And to the man he said, "Because you listened to your wife and ate from the tree about which I commanded you, 'You must not eat from it,' cursed is the ground because of you; through painful labor you will eat of it all the days of your life.

footnotes.text: The opening word is וּלְאָדָם, which lacks the definite article and could be read either as "to the man" or as the personal name "to Adam." Because the surrounding narrative consistently speaks of "the man" and "the woman" as representative figures, and because the personal name is not clearly established until later, this translation reads "the man." The Hebrew idiom שָׁמַע לְקוֹל, literally "listened to the voice of," carries the sense of heeding or obeying; "listened to your wife" preserves the plainness of the Hebrew while implying compliance, rather than flattening it to "obeyed." The phrase בְּעִצָּבוֹן is rendered "through painful labor" to hold together both the toil and the pain in the single Hebrew word; "in toil," "with hardship," and "in sorrow" are all defensible alternatives. The pronoun in "you will eat of it" is feminine in Hebrew and points back to the ground, not the tree — the man will eat from the very soil that has been cursed on his account.

The verse turns on sound and root play. אָדָם ("man") and אֲדָמָה ("ground") are near-twins in Hebrew, so the sentence could be heard as "cursed is the humus because of the human." The word עִצָּבוֹן ("painful labor") is the same rare noun used of the woman in the preceding verse (עִצְּבוֹנֵךְ), binding the two sentences together: her pain comes in bringing forth children, his in bringing forth food. The verb אכל ("eat") sounds three times in this one verse — you ate, you must not eat, you will eat — making the act of eating both the crime and the sentence.

Unlike the serpent in verse 14, the man is not himself cursed; the curse falls on the ground "because of you." The sentence is therefore not simply punitive but relational — human wrongdoing reaches outward into the created order, and human labor is bent from delight into struggle. Some readers stress that the charge "because you listened to your wife" condemns not listening as such but the setting aside of a direct divine command; the accusation is specified immediately by the words "and ate from the tree about which I commanded you." Later biblical reflection picks up the theme of a creation subjected to frustration and awaiting release, and reads this verse as its source.

Several ancient versions appear to have read or interpreted בַּעֲבוּרֶךָ ("because of you") differently, rendering something closer to "in your labors" or "in your works," which suggests a reading like בַּעֲבֹדָתֶךָ. The traditional Hebrew reading, "because of you," is well supported and is followed here; the variant may reflect an early interpretive smoothing rather than a genuinely different text.

The picture assumes the realities of dry farming in the hill country of the ancient Levant: thin soil, dependence on seasonal rain, stones and thorn scrub to be cleared, and the constant possibility of failed harvest. For farmers who heard this text, the words described not an abstract fate but the ordinary shape of the agricultural year — unremitting effort for a yield that was never guaranteed.

text: It will yield thorns and thistles for you, and you will eat the plants of the field.

footnotes.text: The verb is feminine singular ("it will cause to sprout"), and its unnamed subject is "the ground" from the previous verse; the translation supplies "It" to keep that link audible without repeating the noun. Hebrew has two collective singulars, "thorn and thistle," which are rendered as plurals ("thorns and thistles") because English collectives of this kind normally take plural form. The verb is causative and could be rendered "cause to sprout" or "bring forth"; "yield" was chosen for its agricultural ring and its brevity in oral reading. The final phrase, literally "the herbage of the field," becomes "the plants of the field" — wild growth outside a garden, in contrast to cultivated or planted food.

The pair qots wedardar joins two words with matching sound and rhythm — a terse, almost proverbial jingle whose harshness contrasts with the softer vowels of the following clause. Dardar is a rare word, appearing elsewhere in the Hebrew Bible only in a prophetic image of ruined altars overgrown with weeds. The word for the plants eaten, 'esev, denotes low green growth, grasses and herbs rather than trees or fruit. The pronoun "for you" appears in a pausal form of the masculine singular, addressed to the man.

The words describe a changed relationship between humanity and the soil: the ground still produces, but it produces resistance as well as food. Notably the man himself is not cursed — the curse falls on the ground "because of" him — and many readers therefore see here a disordering of vocation rather than a change in human nature. There is also a pointed reversal: in the opening chapters the fruit of trees is given as human food while green plants are assigned to the animals; now the man is told he will eat "the plants of the field," a diet suggesting hardship and a lowered station. Later biblical writers take "thorns and thistles" as a standing image of land under judgment and of fruitless human effort.

Farming in the hill country of the ancient Levant depended on winter rains and constant clearing: thorny weeds such as thistles and spiny knapweed invade fallow or exhausted ground within a single season, and stony terraces had to be reworked year after year. Fields left even briefly untended revert to scrub, so the picture here would strike ancient hearers as an everyday reality rather than an exotic curse. "Plants of the field" also evokes gathering wild greens, a well-attested survival food in lean years.

The Hebrew text of this verse is stable across the manuscript tradition. Ancient Greek and Latin versions render the pair with their standard words for thorns and thistles, and the Greek phrasing was influential enough to be quoted in the New Testament. Some ancient versions make the implied subject explicit as "the earth" or "the ground," reflecting the same understanding assumed in this translation.

text: By the sweat of your brow you will eat your bread until you return to the ground, since from it you were taken; for dust you are, and to dust you will return."

footnotes.text: The Hebrew reads literally "by the sweat of your nostrils (or: face)" — the dual form of the word for "nose" commonly stands for the face as a whole. "Brow" is the natural English idiom for the same picture and keeps the line short and speakable. The word rendered "bread" can mean food in general; "your bread" preserves the concrete image of the staple loaf while still implying daily sustenance. The two occurrences of the same Hebrew particle are rendered "since" and "for" so that the sentence does not stumble over a repeated "because"; both clauses give the reason for what precedes. The closing lines are kept in the word order of the Hebrew — "for dust you are, and to dust you will return" — because the front-placed "dust" carries the emphasis and the balanced cadence reads well aloud.

The verse is knit together by two roots. The word for "ground" (adamah) sounds like the word for "man" (adam), so the man returns to the very stuff he was named for (compare 2:7). And the verb "return" (shuv) occurs twice, framing the second half: "until you return to the ground… to dust you will return." "Dust" (afar) is dry, loose soil or powder, the same word used when the man was formed from the dust of the ground — the sentence closes the circle it opened.

These words are read in more than one way. Many take them as the sentence of mortality: death enters as the consequence of disobedience, an announcement echoed by later writers who speak of dust returning to dust and the breath returning to God. Others read the line as descriptive rather than punitive — a creature made of dust was always destined to go back to dust, and what is newly imposed is the toil, not the ending. Either way the verse binds human labour, human origin and human death together, and it stands behind later reflection on death, resurrection and the hope of a life that does not end in dust.

The picture is that of dry-farming in the hill country of the Levant: rain-dependent grain fields, hand tools, and back-breaking clearing of thorny scrub. Bread from barley or wheat was the core of the daily diet, and "eating bread" was an ordinary way of saying "getting a living." The closing words also reflect burial practice — the dead were laid in the earth or in rock-cut tombs where the body eventually crumbled, and bones were gathered up, so "returning to dust" described something people had seen with their own eyes.

The main ancient translations agree with the Hebrew, rendering "in the sweat of your face you will eat your bread." Some Greek witnesses expand the middle clause slightly, adding "to the earth from which you were taken," evidently harmonising with the wording earlier in the verse; the shorter Hebrew text is followed here.

The final clause has become one of the most widely spoken sentences of the Bible outside of Scripture reading itself: it is pronounced at the imposition of ashes at the beginning of Lent, and its language stands behind the committal at burial services, where earth is cast on the grave with the words "dust to dust."

text: The man named his wife Eve, because she would be the mother of all the living.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew verb הָיְתָה is a perfect form, literally "she was" or "she became." Since no children have yet been born, the statement looks forward, and English renders it naturally as "she would be"; other defensible options are "she is the mother of all the living" (a timeless, titular statement) or "she became the mother of all the living" (viewing the narrative from the reader's later vantage point). The name is given here in its traditional English form, Eve, rather than transliterated as Ḥawwah, so that the familiar name is preserved even though the Hebrew sound-play with "living" is lost. Note also that the Hebrew reads הָאָדָם, "the man," with the article, so the translation keeps "the man" rather than the proper name Adam, which the Hebrew text begins using without the article only later.

The name חַוָּה (Ḥawwah) is explained by a play on the word חַי (ḥay), "living, alive": Ḥawwah sounds like the root חָיָה, "to live." This is a typical Hebrew naming etymology, based on assonance rather than strict derivation. Some scholars connect the name instead to an older root meaning "to speak, proclaim," or to an Aramaic word for "serpent" (ḥiwya), but the text itself supplies the interpretation "life." The phrase כָּל־חָי, "all living," is a collective singular; elsewhere it can include animals, but here it clearly means all human beings descended from her.

The naming stands in striking contrast to the sentence of death just pronounced in verse 19 ("to dust you will return"). Immediately after the curse, the man names his wife "Life" — a gesture read by many interpreters as an act of hope or faith, a first glimmer of promise that human life will continue despite mortality. Others read it more soberly as simply the narrator's way of anchoring all humanity in a single ancestral pair, underlining the solidarity of the whole race in both mortality and blessing. Naming in this narrative also echoes the man's naming of the animals and of "woman" earlier, and interpreters differ over whether such naming expresses authority, insight, or relationship.

Naming a child or person in the ancient Near East was commonly tied to a circumstance, hope, or wordplay rather than to abstract meaning, and mothers as well as fathers gave names. The title "mother of all the living" resembles honorific epithets given to ancestral and goddess figures in surrounding cultures, but here it is applied to an ordinary mortal woman, placing all humanity within one family tree.

The main Hebrew manuscript tradition is uniform here. The ancient Greek translation does not transliterate the name in this verse but translates its meaning as Zōē, "Life," while transliterating it as Heua elsewhere; this reflects the translators' awareness of the Hebrew wordplay. Some ancient versions read "mother of all the living" with a fuller phrase such as "of all living human beings," clarifying that animals are not included.

text: And the LORD God made garments of skin for the man and his wife, and clothed them.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew has three simple verb forms strung together with "and" (made… and clothed), and the translation keeps that chain rather than smoothing it into subordinate clauses, since the plain sequence carries the movement of the sentence well when read aloud. "Garments of skin" renders kotnot ʿor literally; "tunics of hide" or "leather clothing" are equally defensible, but "garments" is the most natural and least anachronistic in English. The noun le-ʾadam lacks the article here, so it could be read as the personal name "Adam"; "the man" is retained for consistency with the surrounding verses, where the same word is regularly definite. The final clause is compressed in Hebrew to a single word meaning "and he clothed them," and the translation matches that brevity rather than expanding it to "put them on them."

The word kutonet (plural kotnot) denotes a body-length tunic, the standard undergarment worn next to the skin; it is the same word used later for Joseph's famous robe and for the tunics of the priests. It is a considerably fuller covering than the ḥagorot, the improvised "loincloths" or "aprons" of fig leaves in verse 7. The verb in the last clause is causative (hiphil): God does not merely provide the clothing but actively dresses them. The Hebrew consonants ʿor ("skin, hide") are homophonous with ʾor ("light"), a resemblance that later interpreters played upon. A paragraph marker in the Hebrew text closes the verse, setting off what follows as a new unit.

The verse is read by many as the first act of divine provision after the judgment: God himself covers the shame the couple had tried to hide, so that mercy accompanies the sentence. Since hides require the death of animals, a long interpretive tradition sees here the first death in the world and an anticipation of sacrifice and atonement, though the text itself says nothing of an altar or offering. Others stress the more sober note: durable animal skins are clothing suited to a harsher world outside the garden, a sign that the human condition has permanently changed. That the same term is later used of priestly tunics has invited readings in which the couple are clothed with a dignity they cannot supply themselves.

Leather and hide garments were ordinary working clothes in the ancient Near East, associated with herders and laborers rather than with luxury; woven linen and dyed wool marked higher status. Clothing in that world signaled role, rank, and belonging, and being clothed by a superior was an act of patronage and honor, as when a king robed a servant. The picture is therefore not of a makeshift covering but of a provision that establishes the couple's standing as they leave the garden.

The ancient versions agree in reading "skin" here, with the Greek rendering "tunics of hide." Rabbinic sources report a reading in one exemplar attributed to an early sage in which the consonants were understood as "garments of light" rather than "garments of skin"; this is best regarded as an interpretive tradition exploiting the similarity of the two words rather than an independent manuscript variant, since no textual witness supports it.

text: Then the LORD God said, "See, the man has become like one of us, knowing good and evil. And now, he must not reach out his hand and take also from the tree of life, and eat, and live forever."

versions.text: Then the LORD God said, "See, the man has become like one of us, knowing good and evil. He must not be allowed to reach out his hand and take also from the tree of life and eat, and live forever."
versions.explanation: The Hebrew opens the second clause with ְוַעַתָּה ("and now"), which marks the turn from observation to action; dropping it loses a rhetorical hinge that also aids oral pacing. The passive "must not be allowed" is wordier than needed and adds an agent not in the Hebrew; the direct "he must not reach out his hand" is crisper for reading aloud. Added commas before "and eat, and live forever" preserve the chain rhythm of the Hebrew waw-consecutives.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew sentence is deliberately unfinished: literally "And now, lest he send out his hand and take also from the tree of life and eat and live forever —" with no main clause following. This broken-off construction (aposiopesis) leaves the divine decision unspoken; verse 23 supplies the action. Rather than end on a dangling clause, which is confusing when read aloud, the translation renders the danger-clause (pen-) as a firm resolve: "he must not reach out his hand." Other renderings keep the fragment ("lest he reach out...") or supply a bracketed conclusion. "See" translates hēn, a presentational particle drawing attention to a fact ('look,' 'behold'); "knowing good and evil" renders an infinitive that could also be read as purpose, "so as to know good and evil." The chain "and take... and eat... and live forever" keeps the Hebrew's unhurried string of verbs, which gives the line its rhythm.

There is a pointed wordplay across the verses: the man might "send out his hand" (yishlaḥ yādô) to seize the tree, so God "sends him out" (wayshallḥēhû, v. 23) of the garden. The same root (šlḥ) is used for the grasp that is feared and the expulsion that prevents it. "Like one of us" (ke'aḥad mimmennû) uses the same plural self-reference as "let us make man" in 1:26. "Knowing good and evil" (lāda'at ṭôb wārā') is a merism — the two poles standing for the whole range — and can denote either moral discernment or comprehensive experience and mastery. "Forever" (le'ōlām) means enduring, unbounded time rather than an abstract eternity.

"Like one of us" has been explained as God addressing the heavenly council of angels, as a plural of majesty or of self-deliberation, and, in later Christian reading, as an intimation of plurality within the Godhead. Some ancient Jewish interpreters read the phrase as "like one who is unique in the world," avoiding any suggestion of comparison. The verse is central to debates about what the man actually gained: a real likeness to God in moral knowledge, or a grasping at autonomy that God's own words concede in part. Note also that the tree of life had not been forbidden; the expulsion is not merely punitive but preventive, keeping the human race from an unending life fixed in its fallen state — a mercy as much as a sentence in much Christian and Jewish reflection.

Trees or plants conferring immortality are a familiar motif in ancient Near Eastern literature: the plant of rejuvenation snatched away from Gilgamesh, and the bread and water of life withheld from Adapa, who is sent back to earth mortal. Against that background, the biblical account is distinctive in that the loss of unending life comes not from a god's jealousy or a hero's carelessness but from a moral breach, and the tree remains guarded rather than destroyed.

The consonantal text is stable across the main witnesses. The ancient Greek and Aramaic versions all read a plural "like one of us," though the Aramaic paraphrases soften it ("like one of us, knowing good and evil, by himself"). The Masoretic accentuation places a vertical stroke (paseq) after "said" and after "and now," marking solemn pauses that the translation reflects with its commas.

text: So the LORD God sent him out of the Garden of Eden to work the ground from which he had been taken.

footnotes.text: The Hebrew opens with a simple narrative connective ("and"), rendered here as "So" to mark it as the direct consequence of God's words in the previous verse. The verb is the intensive (piel) form of a root meaning "send": it can mean anything from "dismiss" and "let go" to "banish." "Sent him out" is chosen partly because the following verse uses a genuinely forceful verb ("drove out"), and the translation keeps the stronger English wording for that stronger Hebrew verb. Hebrew has only a pronoun suffix here ("him"), and the name "the man" is supplied in the next verse; the flow of the reading follows that same pattern. The final clause is literally "which he was taken from there" — Hebrew commonly leaves the resumptive "there" in place after a relative pronoun, which English drops. The unnamed subject of the passive verb is the man himself, recalling his formation from the ground; a minority reading takes the clause loosely as "from where he was taken," with essentially the same sense. The single unbroken sentence keeps the verse readable aloud in one breath-group.

There is a deliberate play on the root š-l-ḥ ("send, stretch out"). In the previous verse God worries that the man may "send out his hand" to take from the tree of life; here God "sends him out" of the garden. The same verb thus turns from the man's grasping to God's dispatching. A second wordplay runs through the verse: the man (ʾadam) is sent to serve/work the ground (ʾadamah) from which he was taken — the pun that also shapes the account of his formation. The verb rendered "work" is the ordinary word for serving, laboring, even worshiping; the same phrase described his task inside the garden, so his vocation is not cancelled, only relocated. "Was taken" is a passive form (a passive of the common verb "take"), leaving the agent unstated in reverent Hebrew fashion.

The expulsion is read in two complementary ways. As judgment, it enacts the sentence already announced: separation from God's presence and from the tree of life, so that mortality becomes irreversible. As mercy, it prevents an endless existence in a broken condition — a life that would be deathless without being whole. Note that the man's calling is not withdrawn: he still works the ground, though now under thorns and sweat. Later biblical tradition reads the scene as the archetype of exile, and Christian readers have seen its reversal in the promise of restored access to the tree of life in the closing vision of Scripture.

A royal garden park, walled and irrigated and tended by a gardener, was a familiar institution in the ancient Near East; to be expelled from the king's garden was to lose both privilege and proximity. Outside such enclosures lay the unwatered farmland, worked with hoe and plow, dependent on rain. The move described here is the move from privileged garden service to ordinary subsistence agriculture — the life the first hearers of this account actually lived in the hills of the Levant.

text: He drove the man out, and east of the Garden of Eden he stationed the cherubim, and a flaming sword flashing back and forth, to guard the way to the tree of life.

versions.text: He drove the man out, and east of the Garden of Eden he stationed the cherubim and a flaming, flashing sword to guard the way to the tree of life.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew phrase 'lahat hacherev hammithappeket' describes a sword that turns/whirls in every direction, not merely one that flashes. 'A flaming, flashing sword' collapses two distinct images (the flame and the revolving blade) into near-synonyms. Rendering it as 'a flaming sword flashing back and forth' preserves the movement of the participle and gives the clause a fuller cadence for oral reading, with a comma pause before the final purpose clause.

footnotes.text: The verb here (wayegaresh) is much stronger than the "sent out" of the previous verse; it is the word used for driving out enemies from the land and for divorcing a wife, so "drove out" preserves the escalation. "East of the Garden" renders miqqedem, which can equally mean "in front of" or "from the east"; the spatial sense fits the eastward orientation of the garden in 2:8 and is the most widely followed reading. Hebrew has "the sword" with the definite article, but English idiom and the flow of the line favor "a flaming sword"; literally the phrase is "the flame of the sword that turns itself." "Flashing back and forth" unpacks a single Hebrew participle describing continuous whirling or self-turning motion. "The cherubim" keeps the Hebrew definite plural rather than smoothing it to "cherubim" or "angels," since the text assumes these beings are already known to the hearer.

The particle 'et before both "the cherubim" and "the flame of the sword" marks them as two distinct objects of the verb "stationed," which is why the sword reads as a separate guarding presence rather than merely a weapon in the cherubim's hands. The verb wayyashken ("stationed, caused to dwell") shares a root with mishkan, "dwelling place/tabernacle," and with the later idea of the divine Presence. The participle hammithappekhet is reflexive in form — "turning itself" — and is feminine, agreeing with "sword" (herev), not with "flame." The infinitive lishmor, "to guard/keep," is the very same verb given to the man in 2:15 when he was placed in the garden "to work it and keep it": the task he forfeited is now handed to the cherubim.

The chapter ends not with annihilation but with a barred door. Access to the tree of life is guarded, not destroyed, and readers across the centuries have heard in that an implicit promise as much as a sentence: what is guarded may one day be reopened. Interpreters differ on whether the exile is chiefly punishment or mercy — preventing an unending life in a broken condition (compare v. 22). The imagery of guarded sanctuary, cherubim, and a way that must be approached from the east reappears in the tabernacle and temple, so that later worship becomes a partial, mediated return to Eden. Christian readers have traditionally linked the reopening of this way to the cross and to the tree of life restored in the closing vision of Scripture.

Cherubim in the ancient Near East were not soft, childlike figures but composite guardian beings — winged creatures with animal bodies and often human faces — set at the entrances of palaces and temples to bar unauthorized approach. Comparable guardian colossi flanked doorways in Mesopotamia and Syria, and related terminology appears in Akkadian sources. Israel's own sanctuary reflected this: cherubim were woven into the tabernacle curtains, overshadowed the ark, and were carved throughout Solomon's temple, whose entrance also faced east. Royal gardens attached to palaces, planted and irrigated by kings, form the everyday background to the picture of a walled, guarded garden with a controlled entrance.

The ancient Greek tradition read the second verb with a personal object — "and he settled him opposite the garden of delight" — making the expelled man, rather than the cherubim, the one who is stationed; the received Hebrew text places the cherubim as the object. Ancient versions also vary in whether the flame and the sword are one thing or two, some rendering "a flaming and turning sword." The Samaritan tradition agrees substantially with the received Hebrew. The verse closes with a scribal paragraph marker (setumah) in the Hebrew manuscripts, marking the end of the section.

This verse closes the opening Torah reading of the annual synagogue cycle. In Christian usage it belongs to the Genesis lessons read at the beginning of Lent and at the Easter Vigil, where the expulsion is set against the announcement of redemption. Eastern churches devote the Sunday before Great Lent to the remembrance of Adam's exile, and hymns for that day take up the image of the closed gate and the fiery sword.
